say: Welcome, wall builders! Today we build a fraction wall and use it to spot fractions that look different but are the same amount, to decide which fraction is bigger, and to add fractions without falling into the bottom-number trap.
Look at the shape. How many equal parts? How many are shaded? Write the fraction on your whiteboard.
How do you know the parts are equal? What would go wrong if they were not?
Which is bigger: one sixth of a strip or one eighth of the same strip? Write a guess before we start.
stuck: Stuck: look at the printed strips, or fold a paper strip in half, then in half again, then again. How many parts now?
For thirds: roll the strip into an S shape until the three parts are the same, or mark every 8 cm.
Ready for more: find three different pieces that together cover exactly one half.

say: “1/3 on the wall lines up with 2 sixths and with 4 twelfths. Same amount, different pieces: 1/3 = 2/6 = 4/12.”
“From 1/3 to 2/6, the top and the bottom were both doubled. From 1/3 to 4/12, both times 4. So 2/5 = 4/10 without a wall.”
“5/6 or 3/4? The parts are different sizes, so I change both to twelfths: 10/12 and 9/12. Now the parts match: 5/6 is bigger.”

do: Ask: “Are the parts the same size? How do you know?”
Ask: “Which fraction did you change, and what did you multiply by?”
Ask: “You added the bottom numbers. Show me on the bar: did the pieces change size?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Find both fractions on the wall. Which one reaches further?”
Hint 2: “Change one fraction so both have the same bottom number.”
Hint 3: “Draw a bar and cut it into the smaller pieces.”

say: “Why is 1/8 smaller than 1/6, even though 8 is bigger than 6?”
ask: “Why is 1/8 smaller than 1/6, even though 8 is bigger than 6?”
The same whole is cut into more pieces, so each eighth is smaller than each sixth. 1/3 + 1/3 is two thirds: the pieces are still thirds, so we add only the top numbers (2/6 is just 1/3).

say: “Today you made the parts the same size before you compared or added. Inquirers check that a comparison is fair.”

p3l6-title.note: Objective: Use a fraction wall to find equivalent fractions, compare and order fractions by making the parts the same size, and add and subtract like and related fractions within one whole. Heuristics taught today: DRAW A MODEL (fraction wall or bar) and MAKE THE PARTS THE SAME SIZE (change one fraction to an equal fraction before comparing or adding). Materials: 7 paper strips per child, all the same length (24 cm works well), ruler, coloured pencils, scissors, mini whiteboards. Online: send the printed fraction strip page instead of asking children to measure and cut strips; marks every 12, 8, 6, 4, 3 and 2 cm give halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, eighths and twelfths. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 5 to 8 (two rounds) and three quick questions 8 to 11, explore 11 to 25 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 25 to 36 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36 to 41, worksheet 41 to 71 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 68 everyone chooses), talk time 71 to 79 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 79 to 85, look back 85 to 88, stamp and close 88 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it.

p3l6-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "show me" ONCE for both: children hold up their paper with both answers in one camera hold-up (about 30 seconds). SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and show them only to the tutor on camera (or everybody holds paper to the camera at the same moment, once for both puzzles). No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): 1/4. Listen for: 4 equal parts, 1 shaded: one quarter. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): No: 1/3 is bigger. Listen for: More equal parts means each part is smaller. Quarters are smaller than thirds. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l6-warm1.note: Minutes 5 to 8. Fraction Flash. Point to one shape at a time. Children count the equal parts (bottom number) and the shaded parts (top number), write the fraction, hold it up, then click to reveal (clicks go left to right). Answers: circle 3/8; rectangle 4/6, which is the same as 2/3 (the 4 shaded parts fill two of the three columns); hexagon 5/6; bar 7/10. Ask every time: "How do you know the parts are equal?" (same size triangles, same size squares). Ask: "What fraction is NOT shaded?" (5/8, 2/6, 1/6, 3/10).

p3l6-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 11. Whiteboards, then click. Ask for a reason each time. Answers: 1) 4. 2) 1/3: the whole is cut into fewer pieces, so each piece is bigger. 3) 5. 4) 6/9: we add the ninths; the bottom number stays 9. Questions 4 and 5 are take-home (2/9 + 4/9 = 6/9; 1 − 2/5 = 3/5): ask only 1 to 3. Watch for children who write 6/18 for question 4: we come back to this mistake later.

p3l6-explore1.note: Minutes 11 to 21. Predict first: "Which is bigger, one sixth or one eighth of the same strip?" Parents cut the printed strips out BEFORE the lesson (the one-week-before message says so), so nobody spends time finding or cutting strips. Pairs only MARK halves, quarters and eighths (fold in half again and again), then compare them with the printed thirds, sixths and twelfths (about 6.5 minutes of pair work). Children label every part (1/2, 1/4 …) and stack the strips. Stress: the parts in a row must be equal, or they are not halves, thirds … Hints: "Which pieces line up with the dashed line at one half?" Ready for more: "Find three different pieces that together cover exactly one half." (with three DIFFERENT pieces the only way is 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12; 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8 repeats a piece). Online: children hold their wall up to the camera. GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): Find 3 DIFFERENT pieces that make exactly 1/2. Is there another way? Answer: Only one way with three different pieces: 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 (3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 6/12). Other ways repeat a piece, e.g. 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8. Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l6-explore2.note: Minutes 21 to 25. Gather the pairs. Answers: 1) 4, so 1/2 = 4/8. 2) 1/6: the same whole is cut into fewer parts, so each part is bigger. 3) No. 2 eighths are too small and 3 eighths are too big. Sixths and twelfths can (2/6 and 4/12). Ask: "What other pieces line up exactly?" Collect a list: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8 = 6/12, 1/3 = 2/6 = 4/12, 1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12, 2/3 = 4/6 = 8/12, 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12.

p3l6-teach1.note: Teach. This is the wall the children built. Run a finger along each row: "Every row is the same whole. Halves: 2 equal parts. Twelfths: 12 equal parts." Ask: "Which row has the biggest pieces? The smallest?" Click: the rule. Say: "The bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole is cut into. More parts, smaller parts. So 1/12 is the smallest piece on the wall, even though 12 is the biggest number."

p3l6-we1.note: Heuristic: DRAW A MODEL. Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "1/3 on the wall lines up with 2 sixths and with 4 twelfths. Same amount, different pieces. From 1/3 to 2/6 the top and the bottom were both doubled: each third is cut into 2, so there are twice as many parts and twice as many shaded. From 1/3 to 4/12, both times 4. So 2/5 = 4/10 without a wall." Ask: "Why must we multiply the top AND the bottom?" (cutting every piece into 2 doubles the shaded pieces and all the pieces).

p3l6-try1.note: Whiteboards up together, then click. a) 3 × 3 = 9, so 1 × 3 = 3: 3/9 (ninths are not on our wall: multiplying works anyway). b) 3 × 2 = 6, so 5 × 2 = 10. c) 6 × 2 = 12, so 5 × 2 = 10. Ask a child to explain c with the wall.

p3l6-we2.note: Heuristic: MAKE THE PARTS THE SAME SIZE. Click through. Think-aloud: "3/7 and 5/7: the parts are the same size, sevenths, so I just count: 5 is more than 3. 2/5 and 2/9: the same number of parts, but fifths are bigger pieces, so 2/5 wins. 5/6 or 3/4? The parts are different sizes, so I change both to twelfths: 10/12 and 9/12. Now the parts match: 5/6 is bigger." The last click shows both as twelfths on equal bars. Ask: "How did I know to use twelfths?" (12 is in both the 6 and the 4 times tables; the wall has twelfths).

p3l6-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) Same top number: sixths are bigger than ninths, so 1/6 > 1/9. b) 2/5 = 4/10, so they are equal. c) 3/5 = 6/10, and 7/10 > 6/10. Ask: "Which rule did you use for each one?"

p3l6-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Adding the bottom numbers as well as the top numbers (1/3 + 1/3 = 2/6, or 1/4 + 1/8 = 2/12). (2) Thinking 1/8 is bigger than 1/6 because 8 is bigger than 6. (3) Comparing or adding fractions with different-sized parts without changing one first (1/4 + 3/8 = 4/8).

p3l6-break.note: Five minutes. Two quarters of a turn is the same as a half turn; four quarters is a whole turn. Online: children stay in view of the camera and turn in place.

p3l6-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 55.5. Walk around. Ask "Are the parts the same size? Which fraction did you change?" before giving any help. In Q1 do (a), (b) and (d) in class: Q1(c) is a take-home question (starred in the workbook). For Q2(g) suggest changing every fraction to twelfths. PAGE 1 CLOCK (41 to 55.5): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 11 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l6-ws1ans.note: Click after a pair explains. Q1(d): 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8 = 6/12; the bottom number is always double the top (top and bottom multiplied by the same number). Q2: (d) 3/4 = 6/8; (e) same top number, sevenths are bigger than ninths; (f) 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. (g) In twelfths: 4/12, 5/12, 6/12, 9/12. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l6-teachadd.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 and Q5). Heuristic: DRAW A BAR. Click 1: the bar cut into sixths; the two teal parts are the third (the 1/3 label sits across both), the yellow part is the extra sixth. Think-aloud: "1/3 and 1/6 are different-sized parts, so I change 1/3 into sixths: 2/6. Now 2 sixths and 1 sixth make 3 sixths. The parts are still sixths, so the bottom number stays 6." Show the mistake: "Ben says 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9. Is a ninth bigger or smaller than a sixth? He drank MORE than 1/3, but 2/9 is less than 1/3. So 2/9 cannot be right."

p3l6-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Watch for adding the bottom numbers in Q4 and Q5. Page 2 is Q4 and Q5 only (Q6 is take-home).

p3l6-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3: B is 2/8 and D is 3/12, both equal to 1/4. Q4: (b) 2/8 + 3/8; (c) 4/12 + 5/12; (d) 5/6 − 2/6; (e) 10/10 − 3/10; (f) 5/10 + 3/10. Q5: 2/3 = 4/6; 1/6 + 4/6 = 5/6; 6/6 − 5/6 = 1/6; 4/6 − 1/6 = 3/6. Q6: 1/4 needs 3/4 = 6/8; 2/3 needs 1/3 = 4/12; 5/12 needs 7/12; 3/8 needs 5/8; 1/6 needs 5/6. Think harder 1: 1/2 = 6/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, so 7/12 and 8/12. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l6-stretch.note: SUPPORT FOR THINK HARDER 1 (this replaces the old teach-between slide; show it only to a pair who chooses Think harder): the number line is cut into 8 equal steps from 0 to 1. Change the ends to eighths: 1/4 = 2/8 and 3/4 = 6/8. In between: 3/8, 4/8, 5/8, so 3 fractions; list them in order and do not count the end fractions. Which of the three is the same as 1/2? (4/8). Answers: 1) 1/2, or 3/6 (1/3 = 2/6, and 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6). 2) 2/5, 1/2, 7/10 (4/10, 5/10, 7/10). 3) 3/10 and 4/10 (1/5 = 2/10 and 1/2 = 5/10; the ends do not count).

p3l6-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 2 ways: 1/2 + 1/8 + 1/8 + 1/8 + 1/8, and 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8. 2) 17/24 (2/3 = 16/24 and 3/4 = 18/24). Another: 25/36 (24/36 and 27/36). Many answers are possible.

p3l6-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Q1: "Start with the biggest piece. If you use a half, what must the other 4 pieces make?" Q2: "The parts are different sizes. How can you cut both bars so the parts match?"

p3l6-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: work in order from the biggest piece, as in the list-in-order puzzles earlier in the program. With a half: the other half needs 4 pieces; 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8 is only 3 pieces, and 1/4 + three eighths is too much, so only four eighths. Without a half: four quarters is only 4 pieces; three quarters + two eighths works; two quarters + eighths needs 4 eighths, which is 6 pieces. Q2: first make the parts the same size: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. There is no twelfth between them, so cut every part in two: 16/24 and 18/24, and 17/24 is in between. Children may cut into 3 or 4 instead (24/36 and 27/36 leave 25/36 and 26/36). The answer is not unique: the ladder of cuts never ends.

p3l6-talk.note: Minutes 71 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Second question if time: "Why is 1/3 + 1/3 not 2/6?" Answer: The same whole is cut into more pieces, so each eighth is smaller than each sixth. 1/3 + 1/3 is two thirds; the pieces are still thirds, so we add only the top numbers (2/6 is just 1/3). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l6-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: No. 1/4 = 2/8, so 1/4 + 1/8 = 2/8 + 1/8 = 3/8. We add the parts, not the bottom numbers. Extension: How many different ways can you fill one whole bar using 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 pieces, as many of each as you like? (9 ways.) Answers are shown only to the tutor on camera (own paper). Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l6-reflect.note: Minutes 85 to 88. Look back: short and safe. SAY: "Turn to the last page of today and find Look back. Tick or write one thing for each line. There are no right answers, and you may pass on any line." Give the children a full 2 minutes, then a short share (the slide has 3 minutes). The page is never collected, marked or read out in front of the group. Children keep their page. The tutor does not see the page, so say: "If something is still puzzling you, you can show this page to a grown-up at home, or tell me at the start of next lesson." At the start of the next lesson, in the open session, invite anyone who would like another look at a puzzle (volunteers only, by hand signal or in the chat; never a private message). Invite volunteers only (one or two) to share something they did well, or what helped. Praise the strategy ("you drew it and that got you unstuck"), not the speed or the answer. Then stamp the journal and close (minutes 88 to 90).
